Flow Switch Setpoint: How to Choose, Adjust and Test the Trip Point on Paddle, Thermal Dispersion and DP Flow Switches

A flow switch only protects a pump or a cooler if its trip point sits in the right place between normal flow and damaging flow. This page shows how to pick that number, convert it to the units on the switch and prove it works.

Paddle, Thermal, DP Deadband and Hysteresis Velocity to m³/h Calculator Adjustment Steps Troubleshooting Table

A flow switch setpoint is the flow at which the contact changes state, chosen between normal flow and the minimum safe flow. Learn how to pick it, convert velocity to m³/h, adjust paddle, thermal and DP switches and test the trip.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how to choose, convert, adjust and test a flow switch setpoint on paddle, thermal dispersion and DP flow switches.
Quick Answer

How to set a flow switch setpoint correctly?

Flow switch setpoint is the flow at which the contact changes state, placed between normal flow and the minimum safe flow, ideally at least 25 % below the low end of normal flow as Gems Sensors advises. For example, 0.3 m/s in a 52.5 mm ID pipe gives Q = v × A × 3600 = 2.34 m³/h, or 46.8 % of a 5 m³/h normal flow.

  1. Find minimum normal and minimum safe flow
  2. Place the trip 25 % below normal, above safe flow
  3. Convert to velocity, paddle setting or DP
  4. Adjust on real flow and read the trip on falling flow
  5. Record as found and as left values

What Is a Flow Switch Setpoint?

A flow switch setpoint is the flow rate, velocity or differential pressure at which a flow switch changes its contact or output state. It is usually set below normal flow so the switch raises a low flow alarm or trips a pump before the process reaches a damaging flow.

Key Facts
  • Gems Sensors advises a setpoint at least 25 % below the low end of the normal flow range
  • Most switches trip on falling flow and reset only after flow rises past the deadband
  • Paddle switches are set by paddle length and a range screw, thermal switches by teach buttons or a magnet
  • Setpoint flow in m³/h = velocity × pipe area × 3600
  • Always prove the trip with a real flow reduction, not only by moving the paddle by hand

If you need a refresher on how the three common designs sense flow, read our flow switch working principle for paddle, DP and thermal types first. This article is its practical companion and focuses only on where to set the trip and how to prove it.

Low Flow Alarm vs Pump Protection Trip

First decide what the switch protects. A low flow alarm warns the operator, while a protection trip stops a pump or heater before damage occurs.

Low Flow Alarm
  • Warns the operator, process keeps running
  • Set closer to normal flow for early warning
  • Short time delay is acceptable
  • Managed under alarm rationalisation rules
Protection Trip
  • Stops a pump, heater or burner automatically
  • Set just above the damaging flow with margin
  • Needs a proven, tested trip path
  • May fall under a safety function review

For alarms, follow the rationalisation ideas in alarm management to ISA 18.2 so the alarm is meaningful and not a nuisance. For trips, the chosen flow switch setpoint must sit above the minimum continuous flow given on the pump datasheet, which our page on centrifugal vs positive displacement pumps helps you read.

A centrifugal pump running near shut off heats the liquid in its casing, as this centrifugal pump working principle guide explains. A minimum flow switch is often its cheapest protection.

How to Choose the Flow Switch Setpoint

Place the trip between minimum normal flow and minimum safe flow, leaving room for switch accuracy.

1
Find normal flow
Take the minimum normal operating flow from the process datasheet, not the design maximum.
2
Find damaging flow
Get the minimum safe flow from the pump, chiller or heat exchanger vendor.
3
Place the trip between them
Gems Sensors suggests at least 25 % below the low end of normal flow, while staying above damaging flow.
4
Allow for accuracy
Gems notes typical switch accuracy of 10 to 20 %, so keep that band clear of both limits.
5
Choose the direction
Decide whether the contact acts on falling flow, rising flow or both.
6
Convert units
Convert the chosen flow to velocity, paddle setting or differential pressure for the switch type.
Setpoint as a percentage of normal flow
% = Setpoint flow ÷ Normal flow × 100
Gems guideline: % ≤ 75 % of the low end of normal
Lower limit: setpoint × (1 + accuracy) above damaging flow
Quick Tip

Write both the normal flow and the minimum safe flow on the instrument datasheet next to the flow switch setpoint. Six months later nobody will remember why 46 % was chosen unless the reason is written down.

Velocity to m³/h: Converting the Trip Point

Thermal dispersion switches are usually specified in velocity, such as cm/s or m/s, while process datasheets give flow in m³/h or L/min. To convert, you need the pipe internal diameter, not the nominal size, because a 2 inch Schedule 40 pipe has an ID of about 52.5 mm.

Pipe area A = π × D² ÷ 4 (D in metres)
Flow Q (m³/h) = v (m/s) × A × 3600
Velocity v = Q ÷ (A × 3600)

The same relationship sits behind our flow rate formula guide, and you can cross check a result with this pipe flow velocity calculator. Use the calculator below to turn a velocity setpoint into a flow and see how it compares with normal flow.

Flow Switch Setpoint Calculator
Setpoint Flow
Setpoint flow 2.34 m³/h (39.0 L/min), 46.8 % of normal flow, a workable margin below normal flow
Solved example: 0.3 m/s in a 52.5 mm ID pipe
A = 3.1416 × 0.0525² ÷ 4
A = 0.002165 m²
Q = 0.3 × 0.002165 × 3600
Q = 2.34 m³/h, about 39 L/min
Normal flow 5 m³/h, so setpoint = 46.8 % of normal

For a DP flow switch across an orifice, remember that differential pressure varies with the square of flow. A trip at 50 % of normal flow therefore needs a DP setting of only 25 % of normal DP, which is a common mistake on site.

DP switch across an orifice or venturi
ΔP_set = ΔP_normal × (Q_set ÷ Q_normal)²
Example: 40 mbar at normal flow, trip at 50 %
ΔP_set = 40 × 0.5² = 10 mbar

Paddle, Thermal and DP Switch Setpoint Methods

Each switch type is set differently: paddles by length and spring force, thermal switches by a taught velocity and DP switches by a pressure setting.

Paddle or Vane Switch

Paddle trimmed to pipe size, then a range screw sets spring force.

Best for: Water, cooling lines, pump suction
Mechanical
Thermal Dispersion Switch

Velocity set by teach buttons, magnet or IO Link.

Best for: Low flows, no moving parts
Electronic
DP Flow Switch

Set as DP across an orifice or filter.

Best for: Gas, steam, dirty service
Pressure
Piston or Shuttle Switch

Fixed by piston and spring, often factory set.

Best for: Small lines, lube oil, hydraulics
Inline

For DP switches the adjustment is the same as on a pressure switch, so our article on differential pressure switch working and our guide to pressure switch setpoint and deadband configuration apply directly. Thermal switches behave like a simplified thermal mass flow meter with a single output.

What Is Flow Switch Hysteresis?

Hysteresis, also called deadband or differential, is the gap between the flow that operates the contact and the flow that resets it. It stops the contact chattering when flow hovers around the trip, in the same way a Schmitt trigger cleans up a noisy electronic signal.

Our article on deadband in pressure switches explains the same idea with numbers, and electronic switches often let you set the reset point separately.

Quick Tip

For a flow proven permissive at pump start, add a start up bypass timer in the PLC. Flow takes a few seconds to build, so without a timer the trip logic stops the pump before it has had a chance to deliver.

How to Adjust a Flow Switch

Set the real flow to the trip value, then change the screw or teach setting until the output just changes.

1
Isolate and permit
Get a permit and bypass the trip under procedure.
2
Check installation
Confirm flow arrow, orientation and straight pipe before touching the setting.
3
Set the flow
Throttle to the trip flow, read on a reference meter.
4
Adjust
Turn the screw or teach until the output just changes.
5
Raise and lower
Increase flow, then reduce it slowly, noting the trip and reset values.
6
Record and restore
Log as found and as left values, remove the bypass.

Dwyer says its TDFS2 learns a setpoint when you tap a target three times with the supplied magnet. The ifm SI series instead teaches a high point at normal flow and a low point at minimum flow with its arrow buttons.

Installation decides whether any flow switch setpoint will repeat. Dwyer asks for at least 12 pipe diameters upstream and 5 downstream for the TDFS2, with the probe inserted 10 to 25 % of the pipe ID, while the FS 2 paddle needs about 5 diameters clear of elbows, valves and pumps.

Myth: A paddle switch trips at the same flow on rising and falling flow
Fact: The FS 2 table shows actuate and deactuate values that differ by a wide margin
Myth: A thermal switch set on water reads the same on oil
Fact: ifm notes oil needs about 2 to 3 times the water velocity and air about 10 times
Myth: Setting the trip very low is the safe choice
Fact: Gems warns that a setpoint set too low can let equipment be damaged before the switch acts
Do You Know?

Dwyer quotes a repeatability of 0.02 m/s plus 3 % of setpoint for its TDFS2 thermal dispersion flow switch. At a 0.3 m/s setting that is about 0.03 m/s, which shows why tiny velocity settings are hard to repeat.

Do You Know?

On a paddle switch the flow switch setpoint shifts if the paddle is bent or trimmed too short. Keep the spare paddle layers, since DwyerOmega uses them to reinforce the vane.

How to Test a Flow Switch

A proper test proves the flow switch setpoint and the whole loop, from sensor to PLC input to final element. Moving the paddle by hand only proves the microswitch, so always reduce the real flow where the process allows it.

  • Reference flow meter or calibrated clamp on meter available
  • Trip direction confirmed: falling, rising or both
  • Trip value read on falling flow for a low flow switch
  • PLC input, alarm text and trip action confirmed
  • As found and as left values logged with date and tag

The routine is close to the one in our pressure switch calibration steps, with flow taking the place of pressure. Check contact use against our NO and NC switch wiring guide, since a protection trip should normally be wired fail safe so a broken wire causes a trip.

Flow Switch Setpoint Troubleshooting

Most faults come from a trip too close to normal flow, poor installation or ignoring the DP square law.

SymptomLikely CauseFix
Trips at normal flowSetpoint too close to normal, or reading rising valueLower trip, check falling flow value
Never trips on low flowPaddle too short or bent, range screw at maxTrim to the correct length, reset screw
Chatters around the tripTurbulence near elbow or valve, small deadbandMove switch, add PLC time delay
Thermal switch driftsFluid temperature or composition changedReteach at current conditions
DP switch trips lateDP set linearly, not by flow squaredRecalculate with the square law

Dwyer adds that changes in fluid temperature, density or viscosity, and the zone between laminar and turbulent flow, shift thermal switch settings.

Flow Switch Setpoint FAQ

What should a flow switch setpoint be set at compared with normal flow?

Set the trip at least 25 percent below the low end of normal flow, as Gems Sensors advises, while keeping it above the minimum safe flow of the pump. For example, with 5 m³/h normal flow, a trip near 2.3 m³/h leaves a good margin.

How to calculate a flow switch setpoint from velocity and pipe diameter?

Multiply the velocity in m/s by the pipe internal area and by 3600 to get m³/h. For example, 0.3 m/s in a 52.5 mm ID pipe gives 0.3 × 0.002165 × 3600, which is about 2.34 m³/h.

Always use the internal diameter, not the nominal pipe size.

What is the difference between setpoint and reset point on a flow switch?

The setpoint is the flow at which the contact changes state, while the reset point is where it returns. The gap is the deadband, and on a DwyerOmega FS 2 in a 1 inch pipe it runs from 4.0 GPM rising to 1.8 GPM falling.

How do you adjust a paddle flow switch to the correct trip point?

Trim the paddle to the length the manual gives for your pipe size, then turn the range screw. On the DwyerOmega FS 2, fully tightening the bolt gives the minimum flow setting.

Set the real flow to the trip value, adjust until the contact just changes and confirm it again on falling flow.

Why does my flow switch keep tripping at normal flow in the pump line?

The usual causes are a setpoint too close to normal flow, turbulence from a nearby elbow or valve, or air bubbles at the sensor. A bent paddle or a dirty thermal probe also shifts the trip.

Check the real flow when it trips, then add straight pipe, a short PLC delay or a lower setting.

Which flow switch type is best for low flow or dirty service?

Thermal dispersion switches suit low flows and clean liquids because they have no moving parts, while DP switches suit gas, steam and dirty service. Paddle switches remain the simple choice for water and cooling lines from about 1 inch upward.

The ifm manual notes oil needs 2 to 3 times the water velocity on thermal switches.
